za-dynasty.s: The Za dynasty was an early ruling dynasty of the Songhai people, centred on Gao in the bend of the Niger River. The Songhai Empire profile notes that a Songhai kingdom under the Za dynasty existed for generations as a tributary state within the Mali Empire.

zabt-system.s: The zabt system was a method of land revenue assessment in the Mughal Empire, developed under Akbar and associated with his minister Todar Mal. Land was measured and classified, and the tax was fixed in cash on the basis of average yields and prices over several years.

zacatecas.s: Zacatecas is a city in north-central Mexico founded after the discovery of rich silver deposits in 1546. It became one of the most productive silver-mining centres of New Spain.

zafarnama.s: The Zafarnama, or Book of Victory, is a Persian chronicle of the life and conquests of Timur, written under Timurid patronage. Versions were composed by Nizam al-Din Shami and later by Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi.

zaghawa.s: The Zaghawa are a people of the eastern Sahara and Sahel, living in present-day Chad and Sudan. Early Arabic writers used the name for the rulers and people of the region around Lake Chad.

zagros-mountains.s: The Zagros Mountains are a long mountain range in western Iran, stretching from the borders of Turkey to the Persian Gulf and separating the Mesopotamian plain from the Iranian plateau. Their highland peoples repeatedly pressed on Mesopotamian states, including the Akkadian…

zagwe-dynasty.s: The Zagwe dynasty was a ruling dynasty of the northern Ethiopian highlands that rose to power after the decline of Aksum, from around 940 CE according to the site's chronology. It is best known for the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, built under its king of that name.

zaju.s: Zaju is a form of Chinese drama combining spoken dialogue, song and music, which reached its classical form under the Yuan Dynasty. Its four-act plays treated historical, romantic and moral themes.

zakat.s: Zakat is the obligatory almsgiving of Islam, one of the Five Pillars, levied as a proportion of certain kinds of wealth and distributed to the poor and other specified recipients. In Islamic states it also functioned as a tax.

zaman-shah-durrani.s: Zaman Shah Durrani was ruler of the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan in the 1790s, a grandson of Ahmad Shah Durrani. He launched several invasions of the Punjab.

zambezi.s: The Zambezi is the fourth-longest river in Africa, flowing from Zambia through Angola, along the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, and across Mozambique to the Indian Ocean. It was a major route for trade between the interior and the coast.

zambia.s: Zambia is a landlocked country in south-central Africa, including part of the Central African Copperbelt. The Lunda Empire profile places the empire's origins in a region spanning the south-east of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo, northern Angola and parts of…

zanata-berbers.s: The Zanata were one of the major Berber confederations of North Africa, many of them pastoral nomads of the Maghreb and the northern Sahara. They played a large role in the politics of the medieval Maghreb, later founding the Marinid and Zayyanid dynasties.

zand-dynasty.s: The Zand dynasty ruled much of Iran from about 1751 to 1794, founded by Karim Khan Zand, a chief of the Zand tribe of the Zagros. Karim Khan governed from Shiraz under the title of Vakil, bringing a period of relative peace after the collapse of the Afsharid Empire.

zanj-rebellion.s: The Zanj Rebellion was a major revolt in southern Iraq from 869 to 883, led by Ali ibn Muhammad and involving enslaved East Africans, known as the Zanj, who laboured in the salt marshes near Basra. The rebels established a state, sacked Basra and defeated Abbasid armies for…

zara-yaqob.s: Zara Yaqob was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1434 to 1468, one of the most powerful rulers of the Solomonic dynasty. He centralised royal authority, reformed the Ethiopian Church and promoted religious literature.

zaragoza.s: Zaragoza is a city in north-eastern Spain on the Ebro River, in the medieval period the capital of an important taifa kingdom of al-Andalus. It was the most important Almoravid city in north-eastern Spain.

zaria.s: Zaria is a city in northern Nigeria, historically the capital of the Hausa state of Zazzau. It became an emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate after the jihad of the early nineteenth century.

zarpanitu.s: Zarpanitu was a Babylonian goddess, the consort of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon. Her statue stood with his in the Esagila temple.

zayyanid-dynasty.s: The Zayyanid dynasty was a Berber dynasty that ruled the central Maghreb from Tlemcen, in present-day Algeria, from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. Of Zanata origin, it emerged from the fragmentation of the Almohad Caliphate.

zeila.s: Zeila is a port town on the Gulf of Aden coast in present-day Somaliland, historically a major outlet for trade between the Ethiopian highlands and the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. The Adal Sultanate profile records that Sabr ad-Din III reconstituted the Walashma state at Zeila…

zemene-mesafint.s: The Zemene Mesafint, or Era of the Princes, was a period of Ethiopian history from 1769 until the mid-nineteenth century, in which the emperors were largely powerless and regional lords held real authority. The Ethiopian Empire profile notes that many emperors occupied the…

zeng-guofan.s: Zeng Guofan was a Chinese scholar-official and military leader who raised and commanded the Xiang Army, which played a central role in suppressing the Taiping Rebellion. He was also a leading figure in the Self-Strengthening Movement.

zengid-dynasty.s: The Zengid dynasty was a Turkic dynasty that ruled northern Iraq and Syria in the twelfth century, founded by Imad al-Din Zengi, who captured Edessa from the Crusaders in 1144. His son Nur al-Din extended Zengid power and sent forces into Fatimid Egypt.

zerafshan.s: The Zerafshan is a river of Central Asia that flows west from the mountains of Tajikistan through Uzbekistan, watering the oases of Samarkand and Bukhara. Its valley was one of the richest agricultural and commercial regions of Transoxiana.

zheng-family.s: The Zheng family was a maritime trading and military clan of south-eastern China, led by Zheng Zhilong and his son Zheng Chenggong, known in the West as Koxinga. Remaining loyal to the Ming, they resisted the Qing conquest and in 1662 seized Taiwan from the Dutch.

zheng-he.s: Zheng He was a Chinese admiral and court eunuch who led seven great maritime expeditions for the Ming Empire between 1405 and 1433. His fleets of large treasure ships sailed through Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa, establishing tributary…

zhizhi.s: Zhizhi was a Xiongnu chanyu of the first century BCE, a brother and rival of Huhanye during the civil war that split the Xiongnu Empire. While Huhanye submitted to the Han Dynasty, Zhizhi led his followers westward.

zhu-wen.s: Zhu Wen was a Chinese military leader who first fought as a rebel under Huang Chao and then served the Tang Dynasty before turning against it. The Tang Dynasty profile records that in 907 he forced the last Tang emperor to abdicate and founded the Later Liang dynasty.

zhu-xi.s: Zhu Xi was a Chinese philosopher of the Southern Song Dynasty and the leading figure of Neo-Confucianism. His synthesis of Confucian ethics and metaphysics, and his commentaries on the Four Books, later became the basis of the imperial civil service examinations.

ziggurat.s: A ziggurat is a massive stepped temple tower built in ancient Mesopotamia and Elam, with a shrine on its summit. Ziggurats were constructed of mud brick, often faced with baked brick, and served as the centre of a city's religious life.

ziggurat-of-ur.s: The Ziggurat of Ur is a great stepped temple tower at the ancient city of Ur in southern Iraq, dedicated to the moon god Nanna. It was built by Ur-Nammu and completed by his son Shulgi in the twenty-first century BCE.

zimbabwe.s: Zimbabwe is a landlocked country in southern Africa, whose name derives from the stone enclosures of Great Zimbabwe. Its plateau was home to a succession of states built on gold, cattle and trade, including the Mutapa Empire and the Rozvi Empire.

zimbabwean-plateau.s: The Zimbabwean plateau is a high plateau in southern Africa between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, rich in gold and suited to cattle herding. It was the setting of Great Zimbabwe and later of the Mutapa and Rozvi states.

zimri-lim.s: Zimri-Lim was the last king of Mari, a city-state on the middle Euphrates in present-day Syria, in the eighteenth century BCE. His palace archive is a major source for the period.

zinkekra.s: Zinkekra is an archaeological site in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya, a fortified hilltop settlement above the Wadi al-Ajal. The Garamantian Empire profile identifies the citadel at Zinkekra as the royal centre of the Garamantes during their formative phase.

zionism.s: Zionism is the nationalist movement that emerged in the late nineteenth century to establish a Jewish national homeland in Palestine. Its political form was founded by Theodor Herzl, whose writings and organisation of the first Zionist Congress in 1897 gave it international…

zirid-dynasty.s: The Zirid dynasty was a Sanhaja Berber dynasty that governed Ifriqiya, roughly present-day Tunisia and eastern Algeria, on behalf of the Fatimid Caliphate after the Fatimids moved to Egypt. The Fatimid Caliphate profile records that between about 1048 and 1052 the Zirid…

zliten-mosaic.s: The Zliten Mosaic is a Roman floor mosaic found at a villa at Zliten, near Leptis Magna in Libya, depicting gladiatorial combat and the killing of prisoners by wild animals in the arena. The Garamantian Empire profile notes that it shows lions and leopards supplied by the…

zoroastrianism.s: Zoroastrianism is an ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of the prophet Zoroaster, centred on the worship of Ahura Mazda and the struggle between good and evil. It was the state religion of the Sasanian Empire, whose kings drew legitimacy from it.

zoskales.s: Zoskales was a king associated with Aksum in the first century CE, the earliest Aksumite ruler named in a written source. The Aksumite Empire profile notes that the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes him as Greek-educated.

zubayrids.s: The Zubayrids were the supporters of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who claimed the caliphate from Mecca during the Second Fitna after the death of Yazid I in 683. For several years they controlled much of the Islamic world.

zulu-kingdom.s: The Zulu Kingdom was a powerful state in south-eastern Africa built by Shaka from the 1810s onward through military reform and conquest. Its rise was associated with the Mfecane, a period of warfare and migration that spread across southern Africa.

zumbo.s: Zumbo was a trading settlement on the Zambezi River, in present-day Mozambique near the borders of Zambia and Zimbabwe. The Rozvi Empire profile notes that gold exports were channelled through coastal trading fairs at Zumbo and Masekesa.

zwangendaba.s: Zwangendaba was a Nguni military leader who led the Ngoni people northwards from south-eastern Africa during the upheavals of the Mfecane in the early nineteenth century. The Rozvi Empire profile records that Zwangendaba's Ngoni crossed the Zimbabwean plateau from…
